strengths: Significance: Preserving clinical information during text augmentation is a useful and consequential problem. Guiding an instruction-tuned generator with entities extracted by a lightweight clinical NER model offers a simple, practical approach.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports substantial improvements in entity preservation and introduction rates across two generator sizes. Table 2 reports the best mean downstream performance across all three tasks for both Qwen and BERT, with particularly encouraging BERT length-of-stay results. The medical-versus-general NER ablation provides some evidence that domain specialization matters.

Presentation: The main extraction–prompting–rewriting pipeline is easy to understand, and Appendix A.1 supplies the proposed prompt. Reporting five-run means and standard errors for downstream prediction is helpful. The discussion appropriately acknowledges dependence on extractor quality and inconsistent results from the DPO extension.
weaknesses: Soundness—clinical safety is not established: Appendix A.3 explicitly evaluates preservation and hallucination using the same entity extractor that supplies the prompt constraints. This measures compliance with that extractor, rather than independently validating clinical fidelity. Entity sets cannot detect changed negation, temporality, drug–dose relationships, or attribution; newly extracted entities need not be factual hallucinations. There is no clinician assessment or independent factual-consistency evaluation. Even the best Table 1 result has PR 0.79 and HR 0.33, supporting relative improvement in a proxy rather than the claimed preservation of critical medical information.

Soundness—selection may confound the evaluation: Appendix A.3 introduces PR/HR acceptance thresholds and discards retrieval-evaluation samples when label-defining entities are absent. Neither threshold values nor rejection rates are reported, and it is unclear whether identical filtering and evaluation samples are used across methods. Consequently, the reported gains may partly reflect filtering or evaluating different subsets rather than better augmentation. Label-dependent filtering also requires clarification about access to ground-truth labels.

Reproducibility is inadequate: The manuscript omits cohort sizes, patient-level train/validation/test splits, class prevalence, note selection and prediction cutoffs, and detailed task-label construction. These omissions prevent assessment of patient overlap and outcome leakage, especially for mortality and length-of-stay prediction. Exact model checkpoints, baseline prompts, generation settings, and DPO training specifications are also missing. Appendix A.3 retains the placeholder 'Training details – add details on SFT and DPO' and conflicts with the main text's training-free collaboration claim by describing updates to both components. Its claimed script release has no identifiable access location.

Evidence for robust downstream benefit is limited: Many Table 2 gains are small relative to the reported standard errors; for example, Qwen mortality improves from 0.911±0.04 without augmentation to 0.917±0.02. Accuracy alone is insufficient to interpret potentially imbalanced clinical outcomes without prevalence, majority-class baselines, and discrimination metrics. Section 6 claims benefits under hospital/time distribution shifts and for rare conditions, but no corresponding shift or subgroup experiments are presented.

Originality and attribution are insufficiently established: The contribution is primarily clinical NER followed by entity-preserving prompting. This could be useful, but the comparisons do not isolate the value of extracted entities from the extensive medical-preservation instructions in the proposed prompt. A matched prompt without the entity list, dictionary extraction, and stronger clinical augmentation baselines would materially strengthen the contribution. The causal framing does not establish that extracted medical entities exhaust the label-relevant variables or that the remaining text can safely be changed.

Presentation and numerical reliability need correction: Table 3 reports naive micro precision 0.138, recall 0.146, and F1 0.149, inconsistent with the standard micro-F1 formula. CATO's HR changes from 0.72 in Table 1 to 0.77 in Table 4 without explanation. Table 3 also does not identify whether it evaluates MIMIC-III-Full or Top-50. These issues reduce confidence in the evaluation.

Limitations and ethics require fuller treatment: The limitations discussion does not adequately address entity preservation versus factual correctness, single-dataset validation, or label-dependent selection. The use of MIMIC notes with GPT-4o and Claude also warrants an explicit description of data handling and compliance with dataset access conditions; the manuscript provides insufficient information to assess this, although it does not establish a violation.

strengths: Significance: Preserving clinical information during text augmentation is a worthwhile problem. Combining a biomedical entity extractor with an instruction-tuned rewriter is simple and potentially useful without requiring a new large model.

Empirical merits: Table 1 shows substantial improvements in entity preservation and introduction rates over both baselines across two generator sizes. Table 2 reports the best mean downstream performance across both model architectures and all three tasks, with five-run standard errors. The BERT length-of-stay results provide particularly encouraging evidence.

Presentation: The core extraction–prompting–rewriting pipeline is easy to understand, and Appendix A.1 supplies the proposed prompt. The paper also acknowledges dependence on expert detection quality and inconsistent results from preference-based distillation.
weaknesses: Soundness—clinical safety is not established. Appendix A.3 evaluates preservation and hallucination using the same entity extractor that supplies the constraints. This measures compliance with that extractor, not independent factual correctness: entity sets cannot reliably detect changed negation, temporal relationships, or drug–dose associations. No clinician assessment or independent semantic validation is provided. Even the best Table 1 result has PR 0.79 and HR 0.33, leaving substantial residual errors under the paper's own proxy metrics. These findings support relative improvements in entity retention, but not the stronger claims of clinically faithful or safe augmentation.

Soundness—downstream evidence needs stronger controls and uncertainty analysis. Several improvements are small relative to reported standard errors; for example, Qwen mortality accuracy is 0.917±0.02 versus 0.911±0.04 without augmentation. Paired comparisons are needed to support claims of reliable gains. Accuracy alone is insufficiently informative for potentially imbalanced mortality and readmission tasks without prevalence, majority baselines, and discrimination metrics. All experiments use MIMIC-III, so Section 6's claims about benefits under hospital or temporal distribution shift are not directly tested.

Reproducibility is materially incomplete. Cohort sizes, patient-level split construction, note inclusion windows, preprocessing, generation settings, and several exact model identities are missing. Without prediction-time note restrictions, mortality and length-of-stay leakage cannot be assessed. Appendix A.3 introduces candidate rejection thresholds without their values or acceptance rates, and label-dependent filtering for retrieval evaluations without explaining its evaluation implications. It also leaves the heading 'Training details – add details on SFT and DPO' and unspecified DPO settings. The appendix's generator/expert fine-tuning descriptions are difficult to reconcile with the main text's training-free augmentation claim. Although script release is asserted, no artifact location is supplied.

Evaluation reporting contains a concrete inconsistency: Table 3 gives Naive micro precision 0.138, recall 0.146, and F1 0.149. Under standard micro-F1, these precision and recall values imply approximately 0.142; F1 cannot exceed both. The ICD evaluation also does not clearly identify which stated dataset variant is reported or sufficiently define how retrieving a grounding rationale determines coding correctness.

Originality and attribution are insufficiently established. The main contribution is entity-conditioned prompting, which could still constitute a useful application contribution, but the experiments do not isolate the value of the expert model. The proposed prompt includes extensive medical-accuracy instructions beyond the entity list. A matched prompt without that list, dictionary-based constraints, and LLM self-extraction would help establish whether model collaboration drives the gains. The causal framing assumes that medical entities capture label-relevant variables without validating that assumption.

The distillation extension is inconclusive. Table 5 primarily compares the distilled pipeline with collaboration and zero-shot prediction, rather than a matched supervised baseline that isolates DPO's contribution. It reports no independent factuality or entity-preservation evaluation of the distilled augmenter. Downstream scores alone do not demonstrate that the model internalizes expert guidance.

Limitations and research ethics need fuller treatment. The discussion acknowledges extractor errors, but does not adequately address relational factual errors, evaluation dependence on the same extractor, or the lack of external validation. Use of de-identified MIMIC-III is appropriate, but the GPT-4o and Claude experiments lack an account of clinical-data handling and applicable access conditions. This is a reporting gap, not evidence of misconduct.

strengths: Significance: Preserving clinical information during text augmentation is a useful and consequential problem. The proposed combination of biomedical entity extraction and constrained rewriting is simple and potentially accessible without training a large domain-specific generator.

Empirical merits: Table 1 shows substantial improvements in entity preservation and hallucination proxies across two generator sizes. For Llama-3.2-3B, preservation increases from 0.62 with CATO to 0.79, while the hallucination proxy decreases from 0.72 to 0.33. Table 2 also reports the best mean downstream results for the proposed method across both predictor architectures and all three tasks.

Presentation: The core extraction–prompting–rewriting pipeline is easy to understand, and Appendix A.1 supplies a concrete prompt. Evaluations cover several clinical tasks, and Table 2 reports standard errors over five runs.

Limitations: The discussion appropriately recognizes dependence on the extractor’s recall and the tradeoff between preserving entities and allowing variation. The authors also acknowledge inconsistent results when distilling the collaboration into a single model.
weaknesses: Soundness—clinical safety is not established: Preservation Rate and Hallucination Rate measure entity-set overlap, using the same extractor that supplies the prompt constraints (Appendix A.3). This favors compliance with the extractor rather than independently verifying factual consistency. Negation, temporality, dosage relationships, and patient attribution can change while entity sets remain unchanged; legitimate paraphrases can introduce apparently new entities. There is no clinician evaluation or independent assessment of these errors. Even the strongest Table 1 configuration retains substantial entity omissions and additions. The evidence supports improved entity retention, but not the manuscript’s broader claims of clinically faithful, safe augmentation.

Soundness—filtering may confound the comparisons: Appendix A.3 introduces acceptance thresholds on preservation and hallucination, plus rejection of retrieval examples whose label-defining entities disappear. Neither threshold values, rejection rates, nor consistent application across baselines are reported. It is therefore unclear how much improvement comes from expert prompting versus selective filtering, or whether methods are evaluated on the same examples. Using label-defining entities for evaluation-time selection also requires explicit safeguards against label-informed selection bias.

Reproducibility: Essential details are missing, including cohort sizes, patient-disjoint splits, note-selection and prediction-time windows, class prevalences, generation settings, and the precise downstream model checkpoints. Prediction-time windows are particularly important because later notes can reveal mortality or length of stay. The main text describes pretrained collaboration without additional training, whereas the appendix says the generalist and weak expert are fine-tuned. Appendix A.3 retains the placeholder 'Training details – add details on SFT and DPO'; DPO parameters are described only as following common practice. The stated script release has no identifiable artifact link in the manuscript.

Strength of evidence: Several Table 2 gains are small relative to the reported standard errors, particularly mortality and the Qwen length-of-stay results; paired uncertainty estimates are needed to establish reliable improvements. Accuracy alone is insufficient to interpret potentially imbalanced mortality and readmission tasks without prevalence, majority-class baselines, and discrimination metrics. Section 6 also claims benefits under hospital or temporal distribution shift, although no corresponding split or external evaluation is documented.

Evaluation integrity: Table 3 reports naive micro precision of 0.138, recall of 0.146, and F1 of 0.149, inconsistent with standard micro-F1, which would be approximately 0.142. The retrieval criterion based on finding a grounding rationale is insufficiently specified, and the table does not distinguish the two announced ICD datasets. These issues prevent a confident interpretation of the coding results.

Originality and attribution: The contribution is principally a combination of existing biomedical NER, preservation prompting, and optional DPO. This can be useful, but the experiments do not isolate the benefit of expert extraction from stronger generic medical-preservation instructions. A matched prompt without extracted entities, dictionary-based constraints, and generalist self-extraction would clarify the added value. Preserving medical keywords also does not establish preservation of causal variables or removal of spurious correlations.

Research ethics: The manuscript uses de-identified MIMIC-III data and evaluates proprietary inference models, but does not explain whether clinical notes were transmitted to external services or how this complied with dataset access and data-handling requirements. This is a reporting gap rather than evidence of misconduct, but it should be resolved for reproducibility and responsible clinical-data use.

strengths: Significance: Preserving clinical information during text augmentation is a useful and consequential problem. Combining a biomedical entity extractor with an instruction-following rewriter provides a simple, potentially practical intervention.

Empirical evidence: Table 2 reports improved token preservation (0.79 versus 0.51 for naive augmentation) and reduced entity hallucination (0.33 versus 0.59). Alternative extractors and evaluators in Tables 3–5 provide some evidence that the improvements are not exclusive to one NER model.

Independent validation: Three clinically experienced nurses evaluated 26 discharge summaries. Their annotations favor the proposed method at both token and concept levels (Table 11). The discussion of missed implicit clinical information usefully acknowledges a real failure mode.

Presentation and utility: The core pipeline and prompt are easy to understand. Table 1 reports the best mean performance across three tasks and two downstream architectures, while Table 12 measures a modest augmentation-time overhead over naive rewriting.
weaknesses: Soundness—clinical safety is not established by entity preservation. Entity-set overlap cannot reliably detect changes in negation, temporality, experiencer, or relationships between medications and dosages. Preserving medical keywords therefore does not establish preservation of clinical meaning or labels. Even the clinician evaluation reports concept PR of 0.79 and HR of 0.20, indicating substantial residual errors. The small annotation sample, without uncertainty estimates or a detailed concept-matching and adjudication protocol, supports relative improvement but not the manuscript's stronger safety claims.

Soundness—the corruption bound in Section 4 requires an unstated assumption. The expression rε + (1−r)pc assumes that unrecognized critical content is corrupted no more often under the constrained prompt than under unconstrained generation. This does not follow from the stated setup: adding constraints can change generation elsewhere. Consequently, the claimed guarantee of no degradation, and the assertion that false positives cannot increase critical-information corruption, are unsupported.

Reproducibility—essential experimental specifications are missing or contradictory. The paper does not specify cohort sizes, patient-level train/validation/test splits, class prevalence, or note availability relative to prediction time, preventing assessment of leakage and clinical validity. Appendix A.3 introduces PR/HR filtering without numerical thresholds, acceptance rates, or clear baseline parity. Appendices A.1/A.3 describe training the generalist and weak expert, whereas the main contribution and Appendix A.5 describe a frozen, inference-only pipeline. Exact decoding, long-context handling, and DPO settings are also insufficiently specified.

Significance and evidential strength—the downstream results are promising but do not establish the claimed robustness. Several gains are small relative to the reported standard errors; for example, Qwen mortality accuracy improves from 0.911±0.04 to 0.917±0.02. Accuracy alone is inadequate to characterize potentially imbalanced mortality and readmission tasks without prevalence, discrimination, and calibration results. Section 6 claims benefits under hospital and temporal shifts, but no corresponding held-out-hospital or temporal-shift experiment is reported.

Originality and attribution—the contribution is primarily an integration of existing NER and constrained prompting. This could still be useful, but the evaluation does not isolate why it works. Missing controls include the identical detailed prompt without the extracted entity list, generalist self-extraction, and dictionary-based extraction. There is also no measured diversity–fidelity tradeoff or copying/resampling control, although simply retaining more source text can improve preservation metrics.

Presentation and consistency—several discrepancies materially impede interpretation. CATO's token PR/HR changes from 0.47/0.62 in Table 2 to 0.62/0.77 in Table 3 without a clearly explained configuration change. Appendix A.3 incorrectly points to Table 2 for generalist variations. The distinction between augmentation models and downstream prediction models is repeatedly blurred, including in the training descriptions. These issues require reconciliation rather than merely editorial polishing.

Limitations and ethics—the acknowledged extractor failures and backbone-dependent distillation results are appropriate limitations. However, the generic impact statement does not address the concrete risk of propagating incorrect synthetic clinical information or explain governance for using clinical notes with the commercial inference models reported in Figure 3. This is a reporting gap, not evidence of misconduct. Overall, unresolved methodological and reproducibility issues outweigh the practical merits.

strengths: Significance: Preserving clinical information during text augmentation is an important practical problem. Extracting medical entities with a small specialist model and incorporating them into a rewriting prompt is simple and potentially useful.

Empirical merits: Table 2 reports improved token-level preservation (0.79 versus 0.51 for naive augmentation) and reduced hallucination (0.33 versus 0.59). Alternative NER evaluators, two downstream model architectures, and annotations from three clinical experts provide complementary evidence. The 26-note human evaluation also favors the proposed method.

Presentation and limitations: The central pipeline is easy to understand, and Appendix A.1 provides its prompt. The paper reports five-run downstream results, hyperparameter sweeps, and runtime measurements. It also honestly identifies an example where entity guidance misses clinically important contextual information and acknowledges inconsistent benefits from distillation.
weaknesses: Soundness—clinical safety is not established by entity preservation. Entity-set overlap cannot detect changes in negation, temporality, dosage relationships, or which findings belong to which clinical context. UMLS normalization addresses synonyms but not these failures. Even the human evaluation reports concept-level PR of 0.79 and HR of 0.20, indicating substantial residual errors. These results support relative improvements on the measured criteria, but not the manuscript's stronger claims of safety guarantees or preservation of domain-critical semantics. The small human study lacks uncertainty estimates and sufficient detail about blinding, adjudication, and concept-level scoring.

Soundness—the corruption bound in Sections 4–5 requires an unstated assumption. The expression rε + (1−r)pc assumes that unflagged critical information remains corrupted with probability at most pc after adding constraints. Prompting can change the entire output distribution, and no argument or experiment establishes this assumption. Consequently, the claims that weak-expert errors cannot degrade safety and that false positives only reduce diversity do not follow. The analysis also does not cover newly introduced clinical information.

Reproducibility and experimental validity: The manuscript does not adequately specify cohort sizes, patient-level train/validation/test splits, class balance, eligible note types, or prediction-time cutoffs. For mortality and length-of-stay prediction, note timing is essential to rule out information recorded after the outcome becomes known. Exact decoding settings, long-note processing, augmentation ratios, and DPO training details are also insufficiently specified. Naming MIMIC-III and reporting selected hyperparameters is not enough to reproduce or audit these experiments.

The implemented intervention is ambiguous. Sections 1 and A.5 describe frozen, inference-only augmentation with no additional training, whereas A.1 and A.3 explicitly describe fine-tuning the generalist and weak expert. Section 5.2 instead describes training downstream predictors. Appendix A.3 additionally introduces PR/HR acceptance filtering absent from the main three-step method, without thresholds, rejection rates, or clarification of whether baselines receive equivalent filtering. These discrepancies prevent attribution of the reported gains to entity-guided prompting and undermine the compute comparison.

Significance—the evaluation does not establish several advertised benefits. All clinical data come from MIMIC-III; no hospital or temporal shift experiment supports Section 6's claims about distribution shifts. Several downstream gains are small relative to the reported standard errors—for example, Qwen mortality accuracy is 0.917±0.02 versus 0.911±0.04 without augmentation. Paired uncertainty analyses are needed to establish those gains. Accuracy alone is also insufficient to interpret potentially imbalanced clinical outcomes without class prevalence and discrimination or calibration metrics.

Originality and attribution: The method is essentially NER-conditioned prompting. This can be a useful contribution, but the broader model-collaboration and causal framing do not establish a substantial methodological advance. The evaluation lacks controls that isolate the extracted entity list from stronger preservation instructions and acceptance filtering. It also does not quantify augmentation diversity: copying the input achieves perfect entity preservation and zero entity hallucination, so safety metrics must be interpreted jointly with meaningful variation and downstream utility.

Presentation and numerical consistency: CATO's token PR/HR changes from 0.47/0.62 in Table 2 to 0.62/0.77 in Table 3 without a clear explanation of the experimental difference. Table 10 reports naive micro precision 0.138, recall 0.146, and F1 0.149, which is inconsistent with the standard pooled micro-F1 calculation. Such discrepancies require correction or explicit aggregation details before the results can be trusted.

Research ethics: The generic impact statement is inadequate for a paper explicitly motivated by clinical safety. The manuscript should explain safeguards governing clinical-note use with external inference services and discuss the consequences of residual synthetic misinformation and subgroup-dependent errors. This is a reporting gap, not evidence of a privacy violation.

strengths: Significance: Preserving clinical information during augmentation is a useful problem. Combining a biomedical entity extractor with an instruction-following rewriter offers a simple, practical approach.

Empirical merits: Table 2 shows substantial token-level improvements over naive augmentation: preservation increases from 0.51 to 0.79 and hallucination decreases from 0.59 to 0.33. Alternative NER evaluators and concept-level evaluation provide additional support.
Clinical validation: Three nurses annotate 26 notes, with results favoring the proposed method (Table 11). The acknowledgment that entity extraction misses implicit critical information is valuable.
Downstream utility: Table 1 reports the best mean results across both prediction architectures and all three tasks. The BERT length-of-stay improvement over CATO is particularly encouraging.
Presentation: The core pipeline is easy to understand, and the appendix provides the augmentation prompt, hyperparameter sweeps, and a measured runtime comparison.
weaknesses: Soundness—safety claims exceed the evidence. Entity-set preservation does not establish preservation of negation, temporal relationships, medication–dose associations, or clinical meaning. Human evaluation still reports concept-level preservation of 0.79 and hallucination of 0.20. These findings support relative improvement, but not the manuscript's claims of safety guarantees or reliable label preservation.

Soundness—the corruption bound in Sections 4–5 requires an unstated assumption that conditioning on expert constraints does not increase corruption of undetected critical information. The claimed no-degradation property and harmlessness of false positives do not follow without this assumption. Preserving selected words also does not guarantee preservation of their contextual meaning.

Reproducibility and attribution: Appendix A.3 introduces PR/HR-based candidate rejection without specifying thresholds, acceptance rates, regeneration procedures, or whether baselines receive equivalent filtering. Filtering directly targets the evaluation metrics, so its contribution must be separated from expert-guided prompting. Dataset sizes, patient-level splits, prediction-time note availability, and detailed DPO settings are also missing.

Presentation and reproducibility: Appendices A.1 and A.3 describe fine-tuning the generalist and weak expert, whereas the main contribution and cost analysis describe frozen models with no additional training. This may conflate augmentation models with downstream predictors, but the distinction is essential. Backbone assignments and differing CATO scores across Tables 2–4 also need reconciliation.

Evaluation: Several downstream gains are small relative to reported standard errors; for example, Qwen mortality accuracy increases from 0.911±0.04 to 0.917±0.02. Paired uncertainty estimates are absent, and accuracy alone inadequately characterizes potentially imbalanced clinical outcomes. Section 6 claims benefits under hospital/time distribution shifts without a corresponding evaluation.

Originality and experimental controls: The contribution principally combines existing NER with constrained prompting. Its practical value could justify this modest methodological novelty, but there is no matched prompt-without-keywords ablation, filtering-only control, or measurement of augmentation diversity to establish what drives the gains.

Research ethics: The generic impact statement does not address the specific clinical risks motivating the work. Because GPT-4o and Claude are used with clinical notes, the manuscript should clarify data handling and access-policy compliance. This is a reporting gap, not evidence of misconduct.

Overall: The promising empirical direction is outweighed by unresolved protocol ambiguities and unsupported central safety claims. These require substantial clarification and controlled evaluation before the contribution can be reliably built upon.
